einzeiler: How a thriving market for bottled animal urine turned wildlife waste into a profitable…
kurzfassung: Entrepreneur Ken Johnson built a successful business selling bottled predator urine to hunters, gardeners, and international clients. Sourced primarily from zoos and game farms, the pungent liquid acts as a natural deterrent against pests like deer, rabbits, and wild boars. Despite mixed scientific results regarding its effectiveness, the unconventional product has sustained his family-run enterprise for nearly four decades.
stichpunkte: Ken Johnson runs a business bottling and selling animal urine under the name PredatorPee.
The enterprise originated from a hunting scent company before expanding into pest control for homeowners.
Between 1900 and 2020, the U.S. deer population surged from 300,000 to 32 million, creating massive demand for natural repellents.
Retailers sell roughly $200,000 worth of coyote and wolf urine monthly on Amazon alone.
Supplies are collected from locations like zoos and game farms via floor drains before being shipped in 55-gallon drums.
International buyers include a Japanese distributor who uses wolf and coyote urine to keep wild boars out of rice paddies.
The product even solved a rabbit infestation at Denver International Airport's long-term parking lot.
Scientific studies on the effectiveness of predator urine as a deterrent have yielded mixed results.

clips.hook: Why gardeners started ordering hunting scents out of season
clips.text: Customer inquiries during the off-season revealed that people were using the scents to protect their gardens from rabbits, sparking a major business realization.

clips.hook: The massive multi-million dollar problem deer created for U.S. suburbs
clips.text: A massive population boom among white-tailed deer led to hundreds of millions of dollars in annual damage to suburban landscaping and gardens.

clips.hook: Why wolf urine works on coyotes even where there are no wolves
clips.text: Even though wolves no longer inhabit most of the United States, their scent triggers an instinctive fear response in coyotes, making it a top-selling deterrent.
